Assistant: Of course, I'd be happy to help! Which sport are you interested in improving at?
User: It's a winter sport, and I've been playing it for a few years now. I really enjoy it, but I feel like I've plateaued and I'm not getting any better.
Assistant: That's frustrating! Winter sports can be a lot of fun. Is it a team sport or an individual one?
User: It's a team sport. We play with four people on each team, and we take turns... doing something. I don't want to give too much away just yet!
Assistant: Ha! Okay, I'm intrigued. Well, in general, improving at a team sport involves practicing your individual skills, as well as working on teamwork and strategy. Can you tell me a bit more about what you're struggling with specifically?
User: Okay, I think I can say that it involves ice... and a stone. Does that help?
Assistant: Ah-ha! I think I'm starting to get a picture! Is it curling, by any chance?
User: Yes! I'm an amateur curling player. I love the game, but I'm having trouble with my accuracy. I feel like I'm always missing my shots, and it's getting frustrating.
Assistant: Curling is a fantastic sport! Accuracy is definitely key. Have you tried practicing your throwing technique, or working on your release?
User: Yeah, I've been practicing my throwing, but I'm not sure if I'm doing it right. Do you have any tips on how to improve my release?
Assistant: Well, one thing that might help is to focus on releasing the stone at the right moment. Try to release it when your arm is almost fully extended, and make sure your wrist is straight. You can also try practicing with different grip pressures to see what works best for you.
User: That makes sense. I think I might be releasing the stone too early. And what about sweeping? I feel like I'm not doing that very effectively either.
Assistant: Sweeping is a crucial part of curling! One thing to focus on is making sure your broom is in the right position, and that you're applying the right amount of pressure. You want to be able to control the speed of the stone, but not interfere with its path.
User: Okay, I think I can work on that. Do you have any other tips for improving my overall game?
Assistant: One thing that might help is to watch videos of professional curlers, and try to analyze their techniques. You can also try practicing with more experienced players, to get a sense of their strategies and techniques. And don't be afraid to experiment and try new things – that's all part of the learning process!

The stones used in the game were initially made of any available stone and were polished to make them slide more easily on ice.

Equipment: The stones used in curling have evolved over time. Initially, they were simply large, round stones from a quarry, but now they are made of granite and have handles for players to grip. The handles also enable players to spin the stone, giving it a more precise direction and speed.

Early versions of the game were played on natural ice, while modern curling rinks are artificially frozen and flattened to provide an even playing surface. User: Hmm, I think I'd prefer something with more wildlife. I've always been fascinated by the natural world.
Assistant: That's awesome! If you're into wildlife, I'd recommend checking out some of the national parks or forests. They usually have a diverse range of flora and fauna. What kind of wildlife are you most interested in?
User: Well, I'm not really sure. I just find all creatures to be fascinating in their own way. But if I had to choose, I suppose I'd say insects.
Assistant: Insects are definitely underrated! They're so crucial to our ecosystem, and there's such a wide variety of species. From butterflies to beetles, each one has its unique characteristics. Are you more into observing them or learning about their habits?
User: Both, I suppose. I love watching them move and interact with their environment, but I'm also curious about their life cycles and social structures.
Assistant: That's really cool! If you're interested in observing and learning about insects, I'd recommend checking out some areas with an abundance of insect life. Maybe somewhere with a lot of flowers or near a body of water?
User: Yeah, that sounds perfect. You know, I feel most at home in environments with an abundance of insect life, where I can observe and learn from the fascinating world of spiders.
Assistant: Ah, spiders! They're definitely one of the most fascinating arachnids out there. I can see why you'd be drawn to them. Have you ever had a favorite spider encounter or a particularly memorable experience with one?
User: Actually, yes! I was on a hike once and saw this beautiful golden orb weaver spinning its web. It was so intricate and delicate, and I was amazed by the spider's precision and patience.
Assistant: Wow, that sounds breathtaking! Golden orb weavers are definitely one of the most impressive spiders out there. Did you know that they can spin up to seven different types of silk, each with its own unique properties?
User: No, I didn't! That's incredible. I can see why you'd be a great AI assistant – you're full of fun facts and trivia!
Assistant: (laughs) Thanks! I try to stay up-to-date on all sorts of fascinating facts. But I'm curious, what do you think it is about spiders that draws you in? Is it their intelligence, their adaptability, or something else entirely?
User: Hmm, that's a good question. I think it's a combination of things, but if I had to choose one, I'd say it's their adaptability. I mean, spiders have been around for millions of years, and they've managed to thrive in almost every environment on the planet. That's just incredible to me.
Assistant: That's a great point! Spiders are definitely one of the most resilient creatures out there. And it's amazing to think about how they've evolved over time to adapt to changing environments. Maybe one day, we'll learn more about their secrets and be able to apply them to our own lives.

User: Exactly! You put it into words perfectly. Now, I'm curious – what are some unconventional elements people have included in their ideal workspaces?

User: An aquarium, that's not a bad idea. But, I think I'd want something a bit more... unusual.
Assistant: Unusual, huh? I'm intrigued. Are you thinking of something that's still related to nature, or maybe something entirely different?
User: Actually, I've always been fascinated by spiders. I know it sounds weird, but I find them really interesting.

Assistant: That sounds incredible. I can imagine it now – a cozy, clutter-free space with a terrarium filled with fascinating spiders. It's the perfect blend of calm and stimulating. Do you have any favorite spider species that you'd want to include?
User: Oh, yeah! I've always been fascinated by the Peacock Spider. They're so colorful and tiny. And I've also always wanted to learn more about the Huntsman Spider.

As I sit and wait in the center of my web, I can feel the vibrations of the world around me. I am attuned to every movement, every sound, every vibration. I can sense the approach of prey from far off and ready my body for the perfect attack.

Materials Needed:

- Yarn or string
- Tape
- Plastic spiders (or other spider toys)

Passage: This message greeted ORblogs visitors Thursday. ORblogs, the Godzilla of Oregon blog round-up sites for the past five years, has shut down - at least for now. Loyal visitors of the web site, which aggregates news, posts and photos from hundreds of blogs around the state, got this surprise greeting Thursday: "ORblogs is Closed. "According to a message posted by Paul Bausch, creator of the site, ORblogs had become too much to handle in his free time, "putting it out of the bounds of a hobby." "I wasn't able to make ORblogs self-sustaining financially (let alone turn it into a job)," he wrote, "and I can no longer devote the time to the site that it needs to grow." Around Oregon's blogosphere, people were lamenting the loss of what Bausch billed as "a running stream of Oregon news, commentary and photography from local weblogs," and trying to figure out ways to save it. Many said the site had become a part of their everyday work, lives and community. Over at Siliconflorist.com, blogger Rick Turoczy wonders if ORblogs can be saved. "Paul built a resource that rallied--and completely codified--the Oregon blogging community," Turoczy posted. "And that, my friends, is far too valuable to let slide by the wayside. "Because it's actually bigger than Paul now. Too large for him to manage single handedly, for sure, but something that needs to continue. For the community. And for Oregon." Turoczy is calling on users to step up to prevent the site's demise. This morning, if the comments under the post are any indication, he's getting plenty of volunteers to help keep the site alive. "I'm interested, although not terribly knowledgeable," posted Kathleen McDade. "I know ORblogs helped drive traffic to our Camp Arrowhead site while we were working to save the camp, and I'm certainly grateful for that." Janet Johnson wrote: "Count me in, too, Rick. Just sign me up for something, and if I can't do it, I'll find someone who will. Thank you for picking up the mantle to help Paul out." Over at Josh Bancroft's Life Stream, the goodbye was short but sincere: "Sad that ORBlogs is closing. Hope the PDX Geek contingent can save it." Question/Instruction: How does Kathleen Power Mears plan to approach her new role humbly, and what kind of feedback has she received since her appointment was announced?

Given material: The veteran educator chosen to lead Catholic schools across the Archdiocese of Boston hopes to build upon a recent stabilization of enrollment and even expand the schools by welcoming students of all kinds, including those who do not speak English and children with special needs, she said Friday.
“My goal is to make these schools so attractive that everybody wants to be there,” Kathleen Power Mears said in a phone interview.
The archdiocese announced Friday that Cardinal Sean P. O’Malley had appointed Mears, 56, to the school system’s top post, which she will assume Sept. 15.
In a statement, O’Malley praised Mears’s achievements and her faith.
Mears replaces Mary E. Moran, temporary administrator for Catholic schools, who assumed the interim position following former superintendent Mary Grassa O’Neill’s resignation last summer after five years on the job.
Mears is currently executive director of the National Catholic Educational Association’s Elementary Schools Department. Previously, she had a 31-year career in the Archdiocese of Indianapolis, where she taught grades 1 to 5 and high school before becoming a principal and then assistant superintendent, she said.
For much of her career, Mears said she has worked to integrate children with special needs into mainstream classrooms. She hopes to continue that work in Greater Boston, and to integrate technology into the classroom in ways that enhance learning.
She will enter the job at a turning point for the archdiocese’s 119 schools and more than 40,000 students. A report released by the Roman Catholic archdiocese last month showed that enrollment had nearly leveled off after years of sharp decline, giving the system its first year with no school closures since 2001.
The archdiocese closed more than 50 schools from 2004 to 2010, but only eight since, according to the report, and enrollment in Boston rose slightly in the past five years.
Mears noted the recent stabilization, but said she is certain “there are more children who would like a Catholic education.” To draw them to the archdiocese’s schools, she plans to set high standards, help students develop “21st-century skills” and to work with partners to let parents know Catholic schools can be affordable.
“Sometimes we don’t tell our story well, and people don’t know that it can be accessible, that there is financial aid,” she said.
Mears also shares with O’Malley, she said, an eagerness to reach out to recent immigrants and speakers of many languages, and she plans to work on both recruiting new students and retention of existing ones.
Mears said she plans to approach the job humbly and learn more about the system before she presumes to tell teachers and principals how to improve it.
In the hours after the announcement of Mears’s appointment, she received several calls from people across the archdiocese asking how they could help her, she said.

We have your new summer job waiting!
Visual Lizard is looking for someone to join our team. If you live and breathe web standards, love looking at the world through XHTML, enjoy defining the things you see around you with CSS while figuring out how to put it all into a PHP array and know how to join multiple tables into a single all powerful MySQL query, we want to talk to you.
This position is in our Winnipeg office and would begin as soon as you can. It will be a 3 month term position with an excellent chance for long-term employment. Our company has always been based on people with passion, imagination and desire. We can teach you everything else.
If you are serious about joining us as we work to change the world, please send your resume, relevant URLs and all time favorite video game to hireme [at] visuallizard [dot] com. We look forward to talking to you.
In an interesting announcement, Google has announced that they will be dropping sites that display AdSense ads but have no real content from their search results.
AdSense,, for those of you that don’t do what we do, is a form of advertising that Google uses. It allows people with web sites to place some code from Google into their web pages. Google then indexes that web site or web page and matches content from that page to matching ads. For example, if you run a web site about web design and you place AdSense ads into it, you are likely to get ads from companies that relate to web design (web hosting, Adobe, Dell, etc...) and when each of those ads it viewed (loaded into the browser) you receive a tiny payment from the advertiser(s). All the money is handled by Google. They collect it from the advertisers and then pay it out to the web sites with ads in them. Very simple and in fact has been a big part of Google being worth billions of dollars.
The search giant has notified a number of Web publishers in the last few days that they will be dropped from its popular "AdSense" program starting June 1.
The cut-off notices jolted the online ad world, where hundreds of thousands of people make money in exchange for allowing Google to place ads on their Web sites.
Google’s AdSense software has made it easy for advertisers to piggyback on any Web site - no matter how obscure - that attracts an audience.
In a nutshell, this is fantastic news. This means that you will no longer get steered into dead-end, link pandering sites that are only trying to get search results (and the related traffic) in an effort to profit from the Ad Sense placement they have on their sites.
For Google’s users this should be awesome news. Search results for common searches should become much more useable. AdSense placement on legitimate web sites will gain better content as people with small campaigns can see their content get into more legitimate websites and not lost in those annoying, no-content-all-link-type of sites. Doug should be even happier than the average Google user.
It’s Wilco. With a new album. Can’t wait.
First off, let’s be clear here, we love our designer friends. We appreciate all of them and what they do so much that we used to believe we ourselves could be designers. Lucky for us we got over that! However, it does happen that from time to time, one of our friends brings us a design that we just look at and weep.
If you have ever had one of those projects that make you cringe when you see the design? We have and we feel for you. Many designers think designing for print and the web are the same. We know otherwise and so do you!
Visual Lizard has in the works, an outlet for you, the programmer, to vent against these designers. We will provide a community for you to get your thoughts and ideas out so that the design community can feel your pain.
Of course, this is going to go both ways, because we know that designers, at times, hand off gorgeous work ready to be made into the next great web site, only to see the finished product look nothing like the original design. Designers, you will also have an opportunity to strike back against the programmer as well.

User: Given the text: UPDATED: Wed., May 2, 2018, 9:53 a.m.
When Kathleen Flinn lost her corporate job at age 36, she cashed in her savings and headed to Paris to fulfill a lifelong dream – to attend the legendary Le Cordon Bleu culinary school.
Then she took the rest of us along for the ride, recounting her adventures in her debut book, “The Sharper Your Knife, The Less You Cry.” The New York Times best-selling memoir chronicles the competitive world of the famous cooking school with Flinn’s tart observations and favorite recipes sprinkled throughout.
On May 12, she joins the Northwest Passages Book Club stage at The Spokesman-Review’s Dorothy Dean Home Cooking Show. In an interview before her Spokane visit, Flinn shares her approach to cooking, her new podcast and advice for home cooks.
What first inspired you to cook?
My grandmother and my parents cooked a lot, so I would attribute my early interest to them. I started cooking dinner regularly when I was 13 years old after my father died. It was just my mom and I and she worked full-time, so I took over making dinner. Focusing on figuring out recipes, going to the store and cooking almost every day really helped me overcome my grief.
What dish or ingredients best represents you?
I can’t discount the influence of Julia Child on my life. She’s the reason I went to Le Cordon Bleu in Paris. When I was little, my parents didn’t let me watch much television. There were basically three or four shows that were considered OK – “Star Trek,” Mutual of Omaha’s “Wild Kingdom,” “Gunsmoke” and anything with Julia Child. It seemed like Julia as on endless loop on our local PBS station in the afternoons, so my sister and I would watch her for hours. I was 11 or 12 when I earned my first Girl Scout badge, which was for cooking, and I made her boeuf bourguignon. Her nephew said that dish was a kind of a touch point for her throughout her life, and I think it’s become mine, too.
What is your approach to storytelling through your food?
Anthony Bourdain once said “I ask people really simple questions about what they eat, and they reveal extraordinary things about themselves.” I think there’s a lot of truth to that. Food is part of our memory, and an essential part of our personal histories. Back when I was starting out in journalism and I was writing obits, I often started an interview about by asking what they served at the wake. I love learning to cook from people from other countries because I think it’s a great way to learn about that culture. So I guess I use it as a means to tell a story; the food is never the end, but a conduit to learning about something else.
What most excites you about your latest project?
I’m super excited about my new podcast. It launches in June and it’s called “Hungry for Words.” It’s basically an excuse to lure really interesting people into my kitchen to talk about food writing. I’m interviewing authors I’ve long admired or whose work I find incredibly interesting. I have been collecting interviews for more than a year so I already have 12 episodes recorded. My first guest will be Alex Prud’homme, Julia Child’s great nephew who co-wrote “My Life in France” with her. We spent more than an hour talking about Julia and how she had a midlife crisis, something I’ve never heard before. How else would I get that experience? So it’s been great fun, and I’m really excited to share it with everyone. Oh, and every episode features a recipe from or inspired by the books my guests have written. I make them on the air, we talk about them and then share the recipe online. You can learn more at cookfearless.com.
What’s your favorite dish to prepare at home?
Pretty much anything. My husband will tell you I’m always cooking. I’m lucky because our house is set up so the living room and kitchen are basically the same place, so I cook while we’re watching TV or a movie. In the winter, I love to make soup. In the summer, I’m all about planking salmon. At breakfast, I love to make omelets. It’s how I use up leftovers.
What’s your favorite piece of advice to share with home cooks?
If you don’t cook or won’t cook, then you end up letting someone else feed you. Too often, that’s multinational corporations who don’t have your health or best interest at heart. So I say, just cook. Don’t be afraid to fail. No one is going to walk into your kitchen and tell you to pack your knives and go home like they do on TV. Also you don’t need a bunch of fancy equipment. Just get a decent knife and a few other essentials. The great thing is that you can find a video online to show you how to cook whatever you want. So just get cooking.
What has been your great food adventure (so far)?
I would say that living in Paris for nearly two years studying at Le Cordon Bleu was the biggest adventure. But there are certainly more in store! Lately, I’ve been eying Italy.

User: Given the text: UPDATED: Wed., May 2, 2018, 9:53 a.m.
When Kathleen Flinn lost her corporate job at age 36, she cashed in her savings and headed to Paris to fulfill a lifelong dream – to attend the legendary Le Cordon Bleu culinary school.
Then she took the rest of us along for the ride, recounting her adventures in her debut book, “The Sharper Your Knife, The Less You Cry.” The New York Times best-selling memoir chronicles the competitive world of the famous cooking school with Flinn’s tart observations and favorite recipes sprinkled throughout.
On May 12, she joins the Northwest Passages Book Club stage at The Spokesman-Review’s Dorothy Dean Home Cooking Show. In an interview before her Spokane visit, Flinn shares her approach to cooking, her new podcast and advice for home cooks.
What first inspired you to cook?
My grandmother and my parents cooked a lot, so I would attribute my early interest to them. I started cooking dinner regularly when I was 13 years old after my father died. It was just my mom and I and she worked full-time, so I took over making dinner. Focusing on figuring out recipes, going to the store and cooking almost every day really helped me overcome my grief.
What dish or ingredients best represents you?
I can’t discount the influence of Julia Child on my life. She’s the reason I went to Le Cordon Bleu in Paris. When I was little, my parents didn’t let me watch much television. There were basically three or four shows that were considered OK – “Star Trek,” Mutual of Omaha’s “Wild Kingdom,” “Gunsmoke” and anything with Julia Child. It seemed like Julia as on endless loop on our local PBS station in the afternoons, so my sister and I would watch her for hours. I was 11 or 12 when I earned my first Girl Scout badge, which was for cooking, and I made her boeuf bourguignon. Her nephew said that dish was a kind of a touch point for her throughout her life, and I think it’s become mine, too.
What is your approach to storytelling through your food?
Anthony Bourdain once said “I ask people really simple questions about what they eat, and they reveal extraordinary things about themselves.” I think there’s a lot of truth to that. Food is part of our memory, and an essential part of our personal histories. Back when I was starting out in journalism and I was writing obits, I often started an interview about by asking what they served at the wake. I love learning to cook from people from other countries because I think it’s a great way to learn about that culture. So I guess I use it as a means to tell a story; the food is never the end, but a conduit to learning about something else.
What most excites you about your latest project?
I’m super excited about my new podcast. It launches in June and it’s called “Hungry for Words.” It’s basically an excuse to lure really interesting people into my kitchen to talk about food writing. I’m interviewing authors I’ve long admired or whose work I find incredibly interesting. I have been collecting interviews for more than a year so I already have 12 episodes recorded. My first guest will be Alex Prud’homme, Julia Child’s great nephew who co-wrote “My Life in France” with her. We spent more than an hour talking about Julia and how she had a midlife crisis, something I’ve never heard before. How else would I get that experience? So it’s been great fun, and I’m really excited to share it with everyone. Oh, and every episode features a recipe from or inspired by the books my guests have written. I make them on the air, we talk about them and then share the recipe online. You can learn more at cookfearless.com.
What’s your favorite dish to prepare at home?
Pretty much anything. My husband will tell you I’m always cooking. I’m lucky because our house is set up so the living room and kitchen are basically the same place, so I cook while we’re watching TV or a movie. In the winter, I love to make soup. In the summer, I’m all about planking salmon. At breakfast, I love to make omelets. It’s how I use up leftovers.
What’s your favorite piece of advice to share with home cooks?
If you don’t cook or won’t cook, then you end up letting someone else feed you. Too often, that’s multinational corporations who don’t have your health or best interest at heart. So I say, just cook. Don’t be afraid to fail. No one is going to walk into your kitchen and tell you to pack your knives and go home like they do on TV. Also you don’t need a bunch of fancy equipment. Just get a decent knife and a few other essentials. The great thing is that you can find a video online to show you how to cook whatever you want. So just get cooking.
What has been your great food adventure (so far)?
I would say that living in Paris for nearly two years studying at Le Cordon Bleu was the biggest adventure. But there are certainly more in store! Lately, I’ve been eying Italy.

Passage: KINGSTON—With all eyes on a Tory civil war, Kathleen Wynne is largely out of sight and out of mind.
Just not out of action.
While the media pay her no heed, the premier is quietly making tracks, popping up at town halls and universities across the province. With a spring election looming, it’s like spring training camp — on campus, on stage, on the road.
Is this the calm before the comeback?
Wynne strides into Wallace Hall at Queen’s University, where nearly 200 students are poised to question her on the state of the province. Stern paintings of past university presidents hang on the wood-panelled walls as the premier returns to the campus where she once studied English and history as an undergraduate.
A soft winter sun streams through the high windows as ceiling fans rotate slowly above, returning heat onto the premier, who is perched on a stool. Global warming, sexual harassment and mental health are top of mind, with the economy a strong undercurrent.
The premier is ready with her answers and her offerings: free tuition for eligible students, free prescription medicines up to age 25, a $15 minimum wage.
She deflects their queries with a recurring rhetorical question of her own, turning the focus onto her political rivals: What’s their alternative?
When a student asks why she opposes the Progressive Conservatives’ proposed carbon tax, Wynne counters that, “actually, the Conservatives are against” their own election platform’s climate change measures.
Watching Wynne over two days of meeting university and college students in Toronto and Kingston, the personal animus tends to diminish in person — even if it hasn’t dissolved in public opinion polls. On campus, the premier’s policies appear to be popular, but is her well-honed town hall skill set transferable to the general electorate?
To make the most of the ongoing Tory storm, Wynne must emerge from a maelstrom of her own making after five years in power. That means confronting the demons that have dragged her down.
Perhaps the demonization ebbs when voters notice that she has no horns on her head nor those horn-rimmed glasses (recently replaced by contact lenses as she hones her public image). Yet no one knows more than Wynne how far she has fallen in public esteem, and how little time is left to recover.
At a lunch stop on her daylong tour, the premier tells me she considered quitting a year ago, when the chorus of naysayers was at its peak.
Still trailing in the polls, and personally unpopular, the dial has barely moved.
“I understand that, and I can’t explain it,” she muses, poking at her half-eaten salad.
She is relentlessly upbeat despite the political downturn, selling her policies during long days of campus tours and town halls in what looks like a dry run for the spring campaign. Undaunted by the risk of embarrassing questions.
Is the premier winning converts among voters? Wynne is surely no Justin Trudeau on tour, lacking the love and buzz of the prime minister, not to mention the fealty of his followers.
Even when she connects with voters, she doesn’t always convert them. When she stops at Toni Parisi’s table at a Queen’s cafeteria, the philosophy student is beaming.
As Wynne moves onto the next handshake, I drop back for a word with Parisi, who tells me she comes from a low-income family that benefits from better tuition and loan programs under the Liberals. All that said, and after all that effort by the premier, Parisi hedges — she still can’t decide who has her vote.
In our interview, Wynne concedes time is running out for a turnaround.
“Yep, I get that — we are very close to an election,” she says, lips pursed.
Despite the appetite for change after so many years of Liberal rule, and her own declining popularity, she is counting on voters like Parisi to look at policy over personality at a time of Tory disarray on key issues.

c83-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: How many boss 302 Mustangs were produced in 1970, and how did that compare to the previous year?: The story has it that the designer of this car whose name was Larry Shinoda was asked about this project during development and at the time it was still a secret so he just responded with he’s working on the boss’s car hence the name boss and it’s stuck and it’s fitting because this car is pretty boss. The boss 302 mustang is an extremely popular car not only for mustang fans but for muscle car fans in general and one of the reasons is because this is the street going version of the Trans-Am Racecar that Ford was obligated to sell to the public to make the Mustang platform legal for trans am racing. The boss 302 debuted in 1969 and was mildly revised for 1970 and the most noticeable change on our car is that it is painted in code “T” which is candy apple red a brand new color for the boss for nineteen seventy. The nineteen sixty-nine cars only came in four colors but for expanded that to more than 16 colors for nineteen seventy which included a special color option as well and they may just over seven thousand boss 302 in the 1970 model year up from just 1628 in 1969 and just over 500 of those were painted red for nineteen seventy.
They ride on special suspension with disc brakes magnum 500 wheels with good year Polly glass GT tires to help improve the handling as well. The GT and a poly glass tire indicates that these are 60 series aspect sidewall tires whereas the regular polygon lass with no GT was a 70 series. And a lowered stance which was all designed to give this car cornering ability as well as high-speed performance.
Another small detail is the elimination of the quarter panel scoops that are normally found right behind the door handles. Those scoops were non functional so designer Larry Shinoda remove them from the boss 302 design. The boss 302 also has less bright trim than the fancier mustang mach 1 package or even some of the base model Mustangs. But the boss wasn’t just an appearance package. The 302 engine was different from the typical 302 in the fact that it had a higher nickel content block for better strength the crankshaft was held in place with 4 bolt main caps and a quick identifier of a boss block our screw in type freeze plugs rather than the press in peace is found on standard 30 tues. Ford claimed the power output to be 290 horsepower at 5200 RPM, but these engines were designed to live at higher rpm and featured a new cylinder-head design to flow more air. Some of the internal parts were carried over from the hi-po 289 engine like the connecting rods, but the crankshaft was a cross drilled forged unit for better strength and durability. The camshaft was a solid lifter design with for 77 inches of lift and 290 degrees of total duration which was designed to pull a lot of air through that large valve Cleveland style heads. The valves sighs actually were reduced in some of the later 1970 cars to aid in lower rpm street driving manners. These cars had domed Pistons which yielded a 10.5 to 1 compression ratio and the fuel mix was sent through a huge Holly 784 barrel carb an aluminum intake manifold and it was lit off by a duel distributor. Many of these cars featured a mechanical rev limiter to keep them alive on the street, and it kind of seems ironic on a race inspire car, but these engines also featured a new smog control system installed from the factory, and as you can imagine most of these systems were removed, but properly restored cars like this one have to feature all the correct smog parts to maintain accuracy.
This car features a 391 rear gear and a four-speed manual transmission, and it was capable of 0 to 60 times in the high six second range and quarter mile times in the mood for teens. It wasn’t the fastest Mustang on the drag strip, but those were approaching big block numbers and this was churned out by a little 302. And after all the boss was designed for the road course and not necessarily the drag strip. Inside you won’t find many luxury amenities in a 70 boss 302, but the bucket seats were supportive and the driver set low in the chassis making it a little difficult to see out of the slope sports roof rear window, but it is one of the most comfortable muscle car cockpits we think we’re ever built.
For nineteen seventy the production numbers increased dramatically on the boss 302 and they made just over seven thousand boss 302 in the 1970 model year up from just 1628 in 1969 and just over 500 of those were painted red.

Power and torque (SAE gross): 290 hp @ 5800 rpm, 290 lb-ft @ 4300 rpm.
Brakes: front: solid disc; rear: drum.
Suspension: front: control arms, coil springs, anti-roll bar; rear: live axle, leaf springs.
Dimensions: L: 187.4 in, W: 71.7 in, H: 50.4 in.
Performance: 0-60 mph: 8.1 sec, quarter mile: 15.8 sec @ 90 mph, 60-0 mph: 112 ft (Motor Trend), April 1970.
Assistant: Approximately 7,013 boss 302 Mustangs were produced in 1970, which is a significant increase from the previous year's production of just 1,628.

Assistant: Yes, the Boss 302 Mustang had several handling upgrades compared to the standard Mustang. It had a unique suspension setup that included a front anti-roll bar and stiffer shocks and springs, as well as a rear anti-roll bar and staggered rear shocks. 

Additionally, the car was equipped with quick-ratio power steering and disc brakes on the front wheels. The suspension improvements gave the car exceptional handling and allowed it to be competitive on the racetrack.

The Boss 302 also came with special Magnum 500 wheels and Good Year Polyglas GT tires that were specifically designed for performance driving. The tires had a higher grip level than standard street tires and improved the car's handling even further.

Overall, the suspension upgrades and tire choices made the Boss 302 one of the best-handling muscle cars of its time. It was designed to handle well on the racetrack, which made it a great choice for drivers who wanted a high-performance car for both street and track use.

Assistant: Really? I didn't know that. How do you like it?

Assistant: Well, it's good to hear that you're doing well in your job. You've always been such a giving person, so I knew you were bound to succeed.

Assistant: I remember when you helped my mom out by picking up groceries for her when she was sick. That was really kind of you.

User: Hi, how are you feeling today, neighbor B?
Assistant: I'm feeling much better, thanks to you, neighbor A. You really helped me out yesterday.
User: Oh, it was nothing. I'm just glad I could help. Do you want some more water or anything?
Assistant: No, I think I'm good. But seriously, you're such a caring person. I don't know what I would've done without you.
User: That's what neighbors are for, right? We have to look out for each other. Speaking of which, have you met any new neighbors lately?
Assistant: Not really, I'm not as sociable as you are.
User: Well, maybe I can introduce you to some of my friends. They're from all over the world, and it's always interesting to hear about their different cultures. Oh, speaking of interesting things, remember the time I found that secret room full of treasure in the park?
Assistant: How could I forget? That was a crazy story.
User: Yeah, it was definitely one of the most exciting things to happen to me. But you know what's not exciting? Having to take a few days off from school to recover from a cold, like I did a few months ago.
Assistant: Oh no, I hope you're feeling better now.
User: Yeah, I'm all good now. It's just frustrating when you have to take time off and miss out on things. But I tried to make the most of my time by reading and catching up on some shows.
Assistant: That's a good way to make the best of a bad situation. And it's great that you're back to your sociable self.
User: Thanks, I'm always happy to be out and about, meeting new people and helping out whenever I can. Like yesterday with you, neighbor B.
Assistant: And I'll never forget it. You're the best, neighbor A.

They can begin an ongoing dialog with requests for additional information and feedback from future emails. This can be captured with a customized form in your website and stored in your database. If your website doesn't have this capability, go to www.dmwebsites.net to see how I use a registration form to capture leads in my web development business. The restaurant can also use this email list for referrals to people they might know. By encouraging sign ups at the site, it dramatically lowers the owners cost of keying in the information themselves. They were very professional, but missed a golden marketing opportunity. Here was a simple and very inexpensive marketing approach integrating two communication channels, your website and event promotion. Your website is, or should be, a very flexible marketing tool. Use it and integrate it in as many creative ways that comes to your imagination. Great suggestion. How would you handle the 'asking' people to go to the website? I was thinking that instead of the coupon you could have the web address and a description of the coupon. You could also have a list of restaurant review sites so people could post reviews if they wanted to. 1. Give the website address to each participant at the event directing them to a specified form set up on the website. There you can do one of two things. C. Redirect them to a landing page that is password protected. You email the password AFTER submitting the requested information. 2. If you do not have form functionality on the site, you can also build an email list by directing them to a service like constant contact. You can set up a registration form with a hyperlink embedded on the site. Constant Contact can create a form that each person fills in. You can then email a coupon to each person that registers. I am not sure having multiple restaurants on a site would create an email list. You can set up a registration form with a hyperlink embedded on the site. Constant Contact can create a form that each person fills in. You can then email a coupon to each person that registers. Can you summarize the missed marketing opportunity that the restaurant had during a recent event?
Assistant: The restaurant missed a marketing opportunity at a recent event by not directing attendees to their website to register for a discount coupon instead of just handing out coupons. This would have allowed them to capture email addresses and build a customer database for future communication, referrals, and feedback. Redirecting attendees to a landing page or using a service like Constant Contact could also have accomplished this. By integrating their website and event promotion, the restaurant could have created a more effective and inexpensive marketing approach.
User: Can you provide me with some examples of how other restaurants have successfully integrated their website and event promotions?
Assistant: Certainly! Here are a few examples:

1. A restaurant in New York City hosted a beer festival and partnered with a local food blogger to promote the event through their website and social media channels. The blogger created a landing page on their website to sell tickets to the event and offered a discount code exclusively to their readers. By integrating with a popular local blogger, the restaurant was able to reach a wider audience and generate more ticket sales.

2. A pizza chain in California held a contest where customers were invited to submit their own pizza recipes through the restaurant's website. The winning pizza would be featured on the restaurant's menu for a limited time. This promotion encouraged customers to visit the website, share their own unique ideas, and engage with the brand in a fun and interactive way.

3. A seafood restaurant in Florida offered a special "catch of the week" dish that was only available for a limited time. To promote the dish, the restaurant created a landing page on their website that highlighted the ingredients, preparation methods, and backstory behind the dish. The page also included a reservation form for customers to book a table and try the new menu item.

Overall, successful event promotions on a restaurant's website should aim to engage and excite customers by offering exclusive discounts, unique content, and interactive experiences. By integrating event promotions with a restaurant's online presence, they can build a loyal customer base and create a memorable dining experience.
User: Can you help me come up with a plan to integrate my local restaurant's website and events in a way that promotes our brand and attracts more customers?
Assistant: Absolutely! Here's a plan that you can use to integrate your local restaurant's website and events:

1. Create a dedicated events page on your website: Build a page on your website where you can list all upcoming events at your restaurant. Be sure to include the date, time, cost, and a brief description of each event. Make sure the page is easy to find and navigate from your homepage. 2. Build an email list: Encourage customers to sign up for a newsletter or email list on your website. Offer incentive such as exclusive discounts, event invites, and interesting content in your newsletters. This will help you to communicate with them and keep them engaged with your brand. 3. Host unique events: Plan special events that are unique to your restaurant, such as a beer or wine tasting, a chef's table, or a themed event. Make sure that you promote these events on your website, through social media channels and email lists. 4. Offer tickets and promotions online: Make it easy for customers to purchase tickets or get special promotions for events online. Embed a ticket purchasing or registration form on your website so that customers can easily buy tickets and be registered for the events. 5. Create interactive online experiences: Offer virtual classes, Q&A sessions on social media, cooking tips or online ordering now that most people are staying home. This will allow customers to engage with your brand in a fun and interactive way from the comfort of their own homes. By following this plan, you'll be able to create a synergistic relationship between your restaurant, events and website. This leads to increased traffic to your website and restaurant, attendance, as well as customer satisfaction and loyalty.
User: Can you help me with step-by-step instructions on how to embed a ticket purchasing or registration form on our website? Is it something that I can do myself, or do I need to hire a web developer?
Assistant: Yes, I can certainly help! Here are some step-by-step instructions for embedding a ticket purchasing or registration form on your website:

1. Choose a ticketing or event management platform that suits your needs. Some examples include Eventbrite, Ticketleap, and Brown Paper Tickets. 2. Create an account on your chosen platform, and create an event or ticket type. 3. Once you've created your event, look for the "embed" or "integration" option. This will provide you with the code that you'll need to embed the ticket registration form onto your website. 4. Copy the code that was provided to you. 5. In the page editor on your website, create a new page or section where you'd like to embed the registration form. 6. In the editor, click on the "Insert code" option (this may be called something different depending on your website builder platform). 7. Paste the code that you copied in step 4 into the "Insert code" field. 8. Save your changes, and your registration form should now be embedded onto your website! If you're unfamiliar with website development or don't feel comfortable embedding the code yourself, you may want to hire a web developer or consultant to help you. Many website building platforms (such as Wordpress or Wix) may have plugins or integrations available that make it easier to embed registration forms or ticket sales onto your site.
User: Provide a list of tips for creating successful Facebook Live videos.
Assistant: 1. Plan your content in advance and make sure it’s relevant and engaging for your audience.
2. Promote your live video in advance to build anticipation and generate interest.
3. Ensure good lighting and sound quality to ensure your audience can see and hear you clearly.
4. Use a catchy title and description to entice viewers to tune in and watch.
5. Interact with your audience during the stream by responding to comments and asking for their opinions.
6. Use props and visuals to enhance your presentation and make it more engaging.
7. Keep your content concise and focused to maintain viewers’ attention.
8. Incorporate a call to action at the end of the video to encourage viewers to share and engage with your brand.
9. Monitor your analytics and feedback to improve future videos and tailor your content to the preferences of your viewers.
10. Experiment with different formats and presentation styles to keep your content fresh and engaging.
User: Hey, these tips are great. Can you give me some more information on lighting and sound quality? How can I ensure that my live video has good quality in those areas?
Assistant: Sure, here are some tips for improving the lighting and sound quality in your Facebook Live videos:

Lighting:

1. Consider your lighting sources: Make sure your lighting sources are positioned in a way that eliminates any shadows or glares that could cause distractions in your video. 

2. Use natural light: Whenever possible, try to use natural light as your main source of lighting. If natural light isn't an option, use soft, indirect light from lamps or overhead fixtures. 

3. Avoid backlighting: Make sure your lighting source is in front of you, not behind you, to avoid backlighting which can make it difficult for your viewers to see you. 

Sound Quality:

1. Use a microphone: Invest in a quality microphone that can help capture clear audio. Consider using a directional microphone to block out background noise as much as possible.

2. Check your environment: Make sure you're filming in a quiet place with minimal background noise. If there are any noises from your surroundings, try to reduce or remove them before starting your video. 

3. Test your sound before starting: Before you start your video, test the audio and make sure you can be heard clearly. 

By following these tips, you can ensure your live video has good quality lighting and sound, resulting in a more enjoyable and engaging viewing experience for your audience.
User: Can you give me more specific examples of how I can use props and visuals to enhance my presentation on Facebook Live? I'm not the most creative person, so any additional help in this area would be great.
Assistant: Sure, here are some specific ways you can use props and visuals to enhance your Facebook Live videos:

1. Use product demos: If you're showcasing a product or service, consider using a prop to help demonstrate its features or benefits. For example, if you're showcasing a new kitchen gadget, use it to cook a simple recipe live on camera. 2. Use graphics and slides: Consider adding simple graphics and slides to your video to make important points or to give some visual differentiation from time to time. 3. Use visual aids: Visual aids can help illustrate complex topics in a more engaging way. For example, if you're discussing a new line of clothes, create a slideshow showcasing different outfits and how they wear on different body types. 4. Use props to create visual interest: Props can help create visual interest and keep your audience engaged. For example, if you're a travel blogger, use an iconic landmark from the country you're featuring as a prop behind you while you talk to the audience. 5. Create a backdrop: A backdrop can not only help make your videos more visually engaging, but it can also help set the tone of your presentation. Consider using banners, posters, or other visuals to create a backdrop that's relevant to the topic you're discussing. Incorporating props and visuals can help add visual interest, provide examples and demonstrate key points, and create an overall better viewing experience for your audience. Be creative and think of ways to use these tools to enhance your presentations and make your Facebook Live videos more engaging for your viewers.
User: Hey, these tips are awesome! Can you please provide me with some tips on how to engage my audience more effectively during Facebook Live videos? I want to keep them hooked throughout the video.
Assistant: Sure, here are some tips on engaging your audience more effectively during your Facebook Live videos:

1. Encourage interaction: Encourage your audience to ask questions, suggest ideas, and share their opinions. Respond to their comments during the video to create a sense of community and keep the conversation going.

2. Use polls and surveys: Use polls and surveys to get your audience engaged and involved in the conversation. It is not just a great way to get feedback but it also keeps the audience engaged and take ownership of the discussion.

3. Use a call-to-action: Use a call-to-action at the end of the video to encourage your audience to engage with your brand outside of the video. Ask them to sign up for your email list, check out your website, or follow you on social media.

4. Use storytelling: Use storytelling to connect with your audience on an emotional level. Share your experiences, share your learnings and make sure your communications have a clear and logical flow. Make it easy for your audience to understand the message you want to convey.

5. Be conversational: Speak to your audience as if you're having a conversation with a friend. This will make them feel more involved and connected to what you're saying.

6. Be genuine: Be authentic and be yourself. People connect with authenticity and they appreciate someone who's genuine.

By engaging your audience more effectively during your Facebook Live videos, you can create a more meaningful and memorable experience for them, and build a stronger connection with your brand.

User: Hey, these tips are great. Can you give me some more information on lighting and sound quality? How can I ensure that my live video has good quality in those areas?
Assistant: Sure, here are some tips for improving the lighting and sound quality in your Facebook Live videos:

Lighting:

1. Consider your lighting sources: Make sure your lighting sources are positioned in a way that eliminates any shadows or glares that could cause distractions in your video. 

2. Use natural light: Whenever possible, try to use natural light as your main source of lighting. If natural light isn't an option, use soft, indirect light from lamps or overhead fixtures. 

3. Avoid backlighting: Make sure your lighting source is in front of you, not behind you, to avoid backlighting which can make it difficult for your viewers to see you. 

Sound Quality:

1. Use a microphone: Invest in a quality microphone that can help capture clear audio. Consider using a directional microphone to block out background noise as much as possible.

2. Check your environment: Make sure you're filming in a quiet place with minimal background noise. If there are any noises from your surroundings, try to reduce or remove them before starting your video. 

3. Test your sound before starting: Before you start your video, test the audio and make sure you can be heard clearly. 

By following these tips, you can ensure your live video has good quality lighting and sound, resulting in a more enjoyable and engaging viewing experience for your audience.

User: Can you provide me with some recommendations for reputable food trucks in the area that cater events?

1. The Grilled Cheese Truck - Specialize in gourmet grilled cheese sandwiches and can tailor their menu to your needs. 2. Kogi BBQ - Fusion Korean BBQ that offers tacos, burritos, and sliders, perfect for a unique twist at your event. 3. The Lobos Truck - Offers a variety of Mexican-American fusion dishes, including tacos, burritos, and bowls. 4. The Green Truck - Known for their organic and sustainable comfort food, such as grass-fed beef burgers and vegan falafel wraps. 5. User: Can you give me more information about the Lobos Truck's menu options? I want to make sure they have something for everyone at my party.
Assistant: Certainly! The Lobos Truck menu is a fusion of traditional Mexican street food with American comfort food. They offer a variety of options that cater to different dietary needs, including vegetarian and gluten-free options. Here are some menu items that may pique your interest:

- Lobos Fries: French fries topped with cheddar, cotija cheese, grilled steak or chicken, cilantro, onions, and salsa. - Buffalo Chicken Tacos: Three tacos filled with buffalo chicken, chopped carrots, celery, cotija cheese crumbles, and cilantro. - Grilled Cheese Tacos: Three tacos filled with Oaxaca, Cheddar, and Cotija cheeses, as well as roasted tomato salsa and fire-roasted Anaheim peppers. - Elote: Grilled Mexican street corn topped with cotija cheese and a smoky mayo. - Mushroom Tacos: Three tacos filled with wild mushrooms, roasted garlic aioli, arugula, pickled onions, and cotija cheese. - Vegan Taco Salad: A bed of romaine lettuce topped with black beans, quinoa, avocado, pico de gallo, and house-made salsa. Hopefully, these menu items give you an idea of the type of food The Lobos Truck offers. You can always contact them directly for more information or to customize a menu that works for your event's needs.
User: These are great suggestions! Can you tell me more about the Green Truck's vegan options? My party has a few guests who follow a plant-based diet.

- Mama Burger: A plant-based patty made with organic quinoa, brown rice, and vegetables, topped with vegan cheese, caramelized onions, and house-made Thousand Island dressing on a whole wheat bun.

- Tofu Salad Bowl: A bowl filled with mixed greens, organic tofu, roasted sweet potato, avocado, and cherry tomatoes, topped with a spicy peanut dressing.

- Vegan Falafel Wrap: A grilled whole wheat wrap filled with crispy falafel, hummus, mixed greens, and pickled onions.

- Vegan Grilled Cheese: Made with house-made vegan cheese, tomatoes, and basil on whole wheat bread.

- Veggie Burger: A plant-based patty made with a mix of organic brown rice, mushrooms, and carrots, topped with house-made Sriracha ketchup, and caramelized onions.

These are just a few of the vegan options available at The Green Truck. They also offer gluten-free and vegetarian options. You can contact them directly to customize a menu that suits your party's dietary needs.

User: These examples help a lot, but could you add some more specific tips for decluttering my space? I always struggle with that part.
Assistant: Absolutely! Here are some specific tips for decluttering your space:

1. Start with a small area: It's easy to feel overwhelmed by the thought of decluttering your entire home. Instead, start with a small area, like a closet or a drawer. This will help build momentum and give you a sense of accomplishment that can motivate you to tackle bigger spaces.

2. Sort your belongings: As you go through your belongings, sort them into three piles: keep, donate/sell, and throw away. Be honest with yourself about what you really need and what you can live without. Remember, less is often more!

3. Consider the KonMari method: This popular decluttering method, developed by Marie Kondo, involves keeping only the items that spark joy in your life. Focus on keeping items that serve a purpose and make you happy, and let go of items that don't.

4. Use organizers and storage solutions: Once you've decluttered your space, use organizers and storage containers to keep your belongings in order. This can include things like drawer dividers, shoe racks, and filing systems.

5. Maintain your space: Set aside a few minutes each day to tidy up your space and put things back where they belong. This will help prevent clutter from building up again and make it easier to stay organized in the long run.

I hope these tips help you declutter and organize your space! Remember, decluttering can be a process, so take it one step at a time and be patient with yourself.

c103-m2.summary: The KonMari method, focusing on keeping only items that spark joy, is a popular and effective decluttering strategy.

User: Write a compelling narrative about a courageous local hero who went above and beyond to improve their community, highlighting their heroic deeds and the lasting impact they had on those around them. Consider incorporating elements of conflict, resolution, and personal growth to make the story engaging and emotionally impactful. Additionally, focus on describing the hero's personality, motivation, and unique qualities to create a relatable and memorable protagonist.
Assistant: If there was one person who could inspire the entire community, it was John. John was a man of unwavering courage and selfless service, whose contributions had transformed the once-neglected and ignored area into a thriving and prosperous community.

Years ago, the community was plagued by poverty, crime, and widespread discontent. People had lost hope, and the future looked bleak. That's when John stepped in; he saw the plight of his fellow citizens and knew that he had to do something to make a difference.

John started small, identifying the problems that the community faced and working closely with his neighbors to find solutions. He organized volunteer groups, cleaned up abandoned lots, and helped families in need. John was always there when someone needed help, often putting his own needs aside to aid those around him.

But his work was not without challenges. He faced resistance and ridicule from those who saw him as an idealistic dreamer. Many doubted his ability to make a difference or accused him of being naive. However, John remained steadfast in his commitment to his cause, believing that change could happen if people had faith and worked together.

Over the years, John's efforts reaped significant benefits for the community. Crime rates dropped, job opportunities increased, and the neighborhood became a safer and more welcoming place to live. People started to believe in their community again, and hope was restored.

John became a symbol of hope and resilience, and had left an enduring impact on the people he served. His unwavering courage and determination had transformed a neglected community into a thriving community where families could raise their children with pride and dignity.

In conclusion, John's incredible dedication and devotion to his community have made him a true hero. He may not have worn a cape or possessed any superpowers, but his actions have inspired those around him and served as an example that anyone can become a hero if they are willing to stand up for what is right. John's selfless actions and inspirational spirit will forever remain a beacon of hope and strength for his community.
User: Wow, that narrative about John was truly inspiring! Can you please add more about his personal qualities and what motivated him to help his community?
Assistant: Certainly! John was motivated to help his community because he saw the struggles and hardships that his neighbors and friends were enduring. He had a strong sense of empathy and believed that everyone deserved to live a life of dignity and respect, regardless of their economic status or background.

John's warm and friendly personality endeared him to everyone he met. He was a natural leader who inspired trust and loyalty in those around him. He had a gift for seeing the potential in people and inspiring them to use their talents and skills for the greater good of the community.

John was also a person of deep faith, and his beliefs played a significant role in his work. He believed that all people were created equal and that it was his responsibility to use his abilities to help others. John never sought personal recognition or reward for his efforts; he simply wanted to make his community a better place to live.

Perhaps most importantly, John's courage came not from a lack of fear, but from his ability to push through his fear and persevere. He was not afraid to face the challenges and obstacles that came his way, whether it was a skeptical community or a lack of resources. John was determined to overcome these hurdles and make a difference.

In short, John's qualities of empathy, leadership, faith, and courage set him apart as a hero to his community. His unwavering commitment to making a positive difference in the lives of those around him serves as a shining example of the power of the human spirit.
